lesson.title: A Nation Pulled Off the Sidelines
lesson.summary: The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor ended two years of American neutrality and brought the United States into World War II as a combatant on two fronts.
lesson.body:
Through the late 1930s, most Americans wanted no part of another European war. Memories of the First World War's staggering casualties, combined with the hardship of the Great Depression, fed a strong isolationist mood. Congress passed a series of Neutrality Acts in the mid to late 1930s meant to keep the country out of foreign conflicts by restricting arms sales and loans to nations at war. Groups like the America First Committee argued forcefully that Europe's troubles were not America's business.

President Franklin D. Roosevelt saw the danger of Nazi Germany's expansion differently, and he worked to support Britain and its allies while formal neutrality held. The Lend-Lease Act, signed in March 1941, let the United States supply Britain, and later the Soviet Union and other Allied nations, with weapons, food, and equipment without requiring immediate cash payment. Roosevelt described the policy as making America the 'arsenal of democracy.' It was a deliberate step short of war, but it tied American industry and interests to the Allied cause well before a single American soldier was sent into combat.

Tensions with Japan grew for different reasons. Japan's expansion into China and Southeast Asia through the 1930s alarmed American policymakers, and the United States responded with economic pressure, including an embargo on oil and scrap metal exports to Japan by 1941. Japanese military leaders saw these embargoes as a chokehold on their war effort and their access to resources, and they concluded that a rapid strike against American power in the Pacific might buy them room to seize resource-rich territory in Southeast Asia before the United States could respond.

That strike came on the morning of December 7, 1941, when Japanese aircraft attacked the American naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, sinking or damaging much of the Pacific Fleet and killing more than 2,300 Americans. The attack shattered isolationist sentiment almost overnight. Roosevelt addressed Congress the next day, calling December 7 'a date which will live in infamy,' and Congress declared war on Japan with near unanimity. Days later, Germany and Italy, bound to Japan by treaty, declared war on the United States, and Congress responded in kind. What had been a policy of cautious support from a distance became direct participation in a global war fought simultaneously in the Pacific against Japan and in Europe and North Africa against Germany and Italy.
